newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada dollar ends weaker amid bond, stock selloff.
newsitem.headline: Canada dollar ends weaker amid bond, stock selloff.

text.p: * Canada's dollar ends sharply lower at C$1.3797 (US$0.7248) on Thursday on selling pressure caused by weakness in bond and equity markets. * Strong selling interest on the International Monetary Market in Chicago also cited. * Longer-term, strong U.S. data and possibility of another Fed rate hike a negative for the unit, analysts said.

Canada's dollar ended sharply lower at C$1.3797 (US$0.7248) on Thursday, hurt by a selloff in both bond and equity markets and growing concern that U.S. interest rates will rise further, analysts said.

"There's been pressure on the Canadian dollar because of the bond market performance," said John Nicholson, a managing director of foreign exchange with Scotia Capital Markets. " "The U.S. has seen a big selloff and the Canadian market has followed them down. Also, equity related sales have pushed (the dollar). Obviously the stock market is lower. Both those factors are pressuring the Canadian dollar."
Canada's benchmark TSE 300 index lost more than 3 percent of its value during the session, while the Canadian long bond fell C$0.90 to C$108.38 to yield 7.278.
Analysts also said there was strong interest by U.S. investors to sell Canadian dollars on the International Monetary Market in Chicago ahead of the long weekend.

"It was mainly led by the IMM. The IMM had an early close so all the weakness led right up into the close," said Harvinder Kalirai, a Canadian analyst with I.D.E.A. Kalirai said a transaction between two U.S. banks was the main source of the dollar weakness.
In the longer term, analysts said there was concern that U.S. economic reports indicating the economy there remained strong could prompt the U.S. Federal Reserve to hike interest rates again.
Analysts said the expectation of such a move would further pressure the Canadian dollar as it was unknown if the Bank of Canada would match another U.S. interest rate hike.
"This divergence in policies could quite well continue, so that's becoming an additional pressure really on the Canadian dollar," said Kalirai.
On the crosses, the Canadian dollar dropped to 1.2131 marks from 1.2285 marks on Wednesday and dipped to 89.56 yen from Wednesday's 90.30 yen.
